```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

Suppose several raters have each watched the same video clips and rated them
continuously as the clips played. Each rater produces one time series per
clip, and all of those series share the clip's timeline. The usual first plot
overlays every series as a line. With 15 raters, this spaghetti plot is
already hard to read: the lines cross each other, and it is hard to tell
where most raters are at a given moment or how far apart they are.

A Chromodoris plot summarizes the series moment by moment instead. At each
time point, it pools the values from every series and draws nested quantile
bands around a center line. By default, the bands hold the inner 50%, 70%,
and 90% of the values, and the center line is the mean (or the median, if
you ask for it). The package has three functions. `chromodoris()` draws the
whole plot in one call, `stat_chromodoris()` is the stat behind it for use in
your own ggplot2 code, and `bin_series()` averages each series within
fixed-width time bins.

## Example data

The examples below use simulated ratings. 15 raters each rate three
60-second clips, labeled A, B, and C, at 10 samples per second. That gives
601 time points per rater per clip. Each rater follows the clip's true
signal, but with their own reaction lag (between 0 and 3 seconds), their own
offset, and noise that drifts slowly over time. Clip C has an abrupt shift at
30 seconds.

```{r}
library(chromodoris)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2)
n_raters <- 15
time <- seq(0, 60, by = 0.1)
signal <- list(
  A = function(t) sin(t / 8),
  B = function(t) 0.8 * cos(t / 5) - 0.3,
  C = function(t) ifelse(t < 30, -0.5, 0.7) + 0.2 * sin(t / 3)
)
ratings <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(signal), function(clip) {
  d <- expand.grid(time = time, rater = seq_len(n_raters))
  d$clip <- clip
  lag <- runif(n_raters, 0, 3)[d$rater]
  offset <- rnorm(n_raters, sd = 0.3)[d$rater]
  drift <- ave(rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.06), d$rater,
               FUN = function(e) stats::filter(e, 0.985, method = "recursive"))
  d$value <- signal[[clip]](d$time - lag) + offset + drift
  d[c("clip", "rater", "time", "value")]
}))
head(ratings)
```

The data are in long form, with one row per clip, rater, and time point
(27,045 rows in all) and columns for `clip`, `rater`, `time`, and `value`.
All three functions take data in this form: a column that identifies each
series, a numeric time column, and a numeric value column.

## One clip

Start with clip A. Here is the spaghetti plot, with one line per rater.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
clip_a <- ratings[ratings$clip == "A", ]
ggplot(clip_a, aes(time, value, group = rater)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4)
```

And here is the Chromodoris plot of the same data. The three arguments after
the data name the id, time, and value columns. They can be given bare, as
here, or as quoted strings.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
chromodoris(clip_a, rater, time, value)
```

At every time point, the stat pools the 15 raters' values and draws bands
holding the central 50%, 70%, and 90% of them. The legend labels each band.
The black line is the mean of the 15 values at that time. `chromodoris()`
also adds a viridis fill scale named "Band" and `theme_minimal()`, and it
returns a ggplot, so you can add your own layers, scales, themes, and facets
to it.

The band edges in this plot are jagged. With 15 raters, the 90% band spans
the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles (computed with R's default method, type 7 in
`stats::quantile()`). So at each time point its upper edge lies between the
two highest raters and its lower edge between the two lowest, and the edges
move whenever those raters move, 10 times per second.

## Binning

The `bin` argument averages each rater's values within fixed-width time bins
before the bands are computed. With `bin = 0.5`, each rater is averaged
within 0.5-second bins, so each rater has 2 values per second instead of 10.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
chromodoris(clip_a, rater, time, value, bin = 0.5)
```

Bin `k` covers the times from `k * 0.5` up to but not including
`(k + 1) * 0.5`, and the binned value sits at the bin's midpoint. Times from
0 to 60 give 121 bins, and the last bin holds only the sample at 60 s.

`bin_series()` applies the same rule to a data frame, so you can look at the
binned data or use it elsewhere. It returns the id, time, and value columns
under their original names, with one row per rater and non-empty bin.

```{r}
head(bin_series(clip_a, rater, time, value, width = 0.5))
```

The times in the output are the bin midpoints: 0.25, 0.75, 1.25, and so on.

Choosing a width is a tradeoff. Wider bins give smoother bands, but they hide
any change shorter than a bin, so the width should be shorter than the
changes you care about. The width is in the units of the time column, which
here is seconds.

Binning also matters when raters were not sampled at the same times. Without
`bin`, the stat pools only the values that share an exact time value, so
series sampled at different times need to be binned before they can be
pooled.

## Several clips

Because `chromodoris()` returns a ggplot, adding `facet_wrap()` splits the
plot by clip.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7}
chromodoris(ratings, rater, time, value, bin = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~clip, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Rating")
```

Each panel's bands come only from that panel's rows. The same rater ids
recur across clips, but each panel is binned and summarized on its own, so a
rater's ratings of one clip never mix with their ratings of another.

In clip C, the bands widen around 30 s, where the true signal shifts. The
raters react to the shift at different lags, so the width there is
disagreement about when the change happened. The plot shows this directly.

## Choosing bands and center

`.width` takes any band widths between 0 and 1, and `center` is either
`"mean"` or `"median"`. Here are two bands, 50% and 95%, around the median.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
chromodoris(clip_a, rater, time, value,
            .width = c(0.5, 0.95), center = "median", bin = 0.5)
```

The `type` argument picks the quantile algorithm (1 to 9), which is passed to
`stats::quantile()`.

## Building from the stat

`stat_chromodoris()` can be used in any ggplot pipeline. For each time point
and band, it returns `level` (a factor such as `"90%"`), `.width`, `ymin`,
`ymax`, and `center`. Map `fill = after_stat(level)` to shade the bands. A
second layer with `geom = "line"` draws the center line, because the stat
sets `y` to the center. The center does not depend on the band, so that
layer needs only one value of `.width`.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(clip_a, aes(time, value, group = rater)) +
  stat_chromodoris(aes(fill = after_stat(level)), bin = 0.5) +
  stat_chromodoris(geom = "line", .width = 0.9, bin = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", name = "Band") +
  theme_classic()
```

With `bin` set, the stat needs `group` mapped to the rater id, because each
rater is binned on its own. Without a group, it signals an error.
`chromodoris()` maps `group` for you.

## What the bands do not show

The bands summarize whichever values are present at each time point. This
has a few consequences to keep in mind when reading them.

If the raters' series have different lengths, the bands near the ends come
from fewer raters and can look narrower for that reason alone. The plot does
not mark how many raters contribute at each time.

If ratings sit at a floor or ceiling of the rating scale, such as the bottom
of a -4 to 4 scale, the outer band edges can lie flat on that bound and
understate the spread.

The bands are also not smoothed. Jagged edges reflect the data and the
sampling rate, and binning is the package's tool for dealing with them.
